questions.q: According to this lesson, what are the three things to find first in any unfamiliar API's documentation?
options: The company's founding date, its stock price, and its logo
Base URL & auth, the available endpoints, and which parameters are required
The programming language the API server is written in
The number of other companies that use the API
questions.explain: Those three questions — where to send requests, what resources exist, and what's required — are the fastest way into unfamiliar documentation.

questions.q: In the Swagger UI documentation screenshot, what does the color coding on each endpoint (green, orange, blue) represent?
options: How popular each endpoint is
The HTTP method — e.g. green for POST, orange for PUT, blue for GET
Whether the endpoint requires payment
The response time of each endpoint
questions.explain: Swagger UI color-codes each endpoint row by its HTTP method, a convention that shows up across many documentation tools.

questions.q: In the expanded endpoint documentation, the "status" parameter was marked required, typed array<string>, and sent as a query parameter. What commonly happens if a required parameter like this is missing from a request?
options: The request always succeeds anyway with default values
The server ignores the omission silently
It's one of the most common causes of a 400 Bad Request
The API automatically generates the missing value
questions.explain: Omitting a required parameter is a classic cause of a 400 Bad Request — the request is malformed because something mandatory is missing.

questions.q: Why does this lesson show documentation from two different tools/sites (Swagger UI and another docs page)?
options: To prove that only one of the two is trustworthy
Because different tools generate completely unrelated documentation with no shared structure
To show that once you know what to look for (base URL, endpoints, required params), you can read almost any API's docs regardless of which tool generated them
Because the two tools require different programming languages to use
questions.explain: Despite different visual designs, both documentation sites answer the same underlying questions — required headers/params, types, and valid values.

questions.q: Translating documentation into a real request, what does 'GET /pet/findByStatus?status=available' combine, per this lesson?
options: A random guess at the endpoint with no documentation involved
The documented method and URL, plus the required query parameter's value
Only the response body format, with no method or URL
A POST request disguised as a GET
questions.explain: Reading documentation means taking the documented method, URL, and required parameters and assembling them into the real request you send — the exact anatomy taught in Lesson 4.
